This document contains the analysis scripts and report for the manuscript “A Course on AI for Pre-Service STEM and Language Teachers: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Learning Outcomes Using Intelligent-TPACK and AI Literacy Instruments”. The R scripts and data are hosted at .

library(this.path)
library(dplyr) #e.g. for select
library(tidyr) # for reshaping data
library(stringdist) #levenshtein
library(stringr) # for reshaping data
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)
library(modelsummary)
library(kableExtra)
library(arsenal)
library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggsci) # color palettes
library(jtools) # theme_apa etc.
library(papaja) # for apa reporting

load(file = "data/env-analysis.RData")
is_word <- !(knitr::is_html_output() | knitr::is_latex_output())

if (is_word) {
  library(flextable)
}

modelsummary_output <- ifelse(
  knitr::is_latex_output(),
  "latex_tabular",
  ifelse(knitr::is_html_output(), "kableExtra", "flextable")
)

adjust_table_for_word <- function(ft, width=0) {
  ft <- flextable::autofit(ft)
  ft <- flextable::set_table_properties(ft, layout = "autofit", width=width)
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = 10, part = "header")
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = 8, part = "body")
  ft
}

1 Methods

1.1 Participants

The final sample size included in the analyses was \(n=76\) and is listed in Table 1.

# render as table
format <- ifelse(
  knitr::is_html_output(),
  "markdown",
  ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "latex", "markdown")
)

var_names <- list(
  gender = "Gender",
  age = "Age",
  semester = "Semester Number",
  student = "Graduate Level",
  isp = "Completed Integrated Semester Internship",
  subject1 = "Subject 1",
  subject2 = "Subject 2",
  studies = "Study Program",
  location = "University",
  TK = "Intelligent TK",
  TCK = "Intelligent TCK",
  TPK = "Intelligent TPK",
  TPACK_total = "Intelligent TPACK",
  AILIT = "AI Literacy",
  PU = "Perceived Usefulness",
  Ethics = "AI Ethics"
)

kable(
  summary(
    tableby(
      intervention ~
        location +
          age +
          gender +
          semester +
          studies +
          TK +
          TCK +
          TPK +
          TPACK_total +
          Ethics +
          AILIT +
          PU,
      data %>% filter(time == "pre") %>% droplevels(),
      cat.test = "chisq",
      chisq.correct = T,
      control = tableby.control(test = T, total = T, digits = 2)
    ),
    labelTranslations = var_names,
    pfootnote = T,
    text = F
  ),
  escape = T,
  format = format,
  booktabs = T
)

1.2 Materials

1.2.1 Translation Process

The Intelligent-TPACK, originally developed by Celik (2023), is widely used to assess teachers’ knowledge for pedagogical and ethical AI use based on the technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework.

However, no empirically validated German translations of the Intelligent-TPACK exists. While some studies translate and use subsets of the Intelligent-TPACK (e.g., Mah & Groß, 2024), there is no validated German version of the full instrument.

Therefore, for the Intelligent-TPACK by Celik (2023) as well as items from the AI ethics subscale from Chiu et al. (2024), we translated the original items in a participative multi-step process involving not just experts from the fields of computer science and education, but also (pre-service) teachers. For this, we applied the Modified Direct Translation that includes translators and experts discussing the wording until reaching agreement (Behling & Law, 2025): First, seven researchers and experts in AI ED (additionally including one English teacher and one student teacher of Computer Science and English) translated the items independently. Second, we compared all translations and marked the items that received different translations. In a third step, we performed a group workshop in which the marked items were discussed and dot voting was applied to decide on the most apporopriate translation. Finally, three items that were still marked as questionable were discussed and further adapted with a native English teacher who teaches at University 2.

The translation and validation of the Intelligent-TPACK is reported in detail in Authors (in prep.).

1.3 Analysis

We analyzed the interventions’ efficacy in a multilevel analysis approach. To contrast the differences of students’ change in the respective outcome measure over time, we implemented a linear mixed-effects regression model for each outcome measure, considering our \(3\) factorial design. To account for the panel structure, that is, two test sessions, in the data, we used the random effects (RE) estimation method to estimate treatment effects, following CITATION.

Note

Ist unser Design 3- oder 2-faktoriell?

We implemented the two-level models with the students at level 1 (individual level) and the University at level 2 (class level). We addressed the clustering of time points within students by including random intercepts for students. The clustering of students within universities was addressed by including a dummy variable for the University.

To contrast the differences in change over time between the treatment groups (i.e., estimated treatment effect), we included the time-by-treatment interaction in the models. For this, we used a dummy-coded treatment variable using reversed Helmert contrasts to contrast the differences between (i) the control group and the intervention groups and (ii) between the two intervention groups. We set the control group as the reference group.

Finally, we included variables as a covariate if they met the criteria for baseline equivalence in randomized controlled trials by the What Works Clearinghouse (Clearinghouse, 2022). That is, we included the variables as covariates if the difference between the groups was statistical significant, or if it exceeded \(d>.05\). We tested for group differences concerning the following variables at baseline (pretest): age, semester, gender, study level (Bachelor vs. Master). We found for all variables either statistically significant differences or differences larger than \(d=.05\), see Table 1. That is, we included the following covariates in the models: XYZ.

That is, the final model for each outcome measure contained time, treatment, XYZ, University and the interaction of time and treatment as fixed effects and a random intercept for students, and was specified as follows: lmer(outcome ~ time * treatment + age + semester + universty + (1|student)).

The criterion of statistical significance was set at α=.05.

Note

Semesterzahl oder Studienlevel (Bachelor vs. Master) als Kovariate?

1.3.1 Statistical Software

We performed the statistical analyses in R (R Core Team, 2024) using the following packages: dplyr [wickham2023:dplyr], tidyr (Wickham et al., 2024), and gtools (Warnes et al., 2023) for data wrangling; arsenal (Heinzen et al., 2021), vtable (Huntington-Klein, 2023), modelsummary (Arel-Bundock, 2022) and kableExtra (Zhu, 2024) for creating tables; ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016), ggsci (Xiao, 2024) and jtools (Long, 2022) for plotting; and lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) for linear mixed-effects regression analyses.

We used the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) to fit linear mixed-effects models and the broom.mixed package (Bolker & Robinson, 2024) to extract the results. Degrees of freedom and p-values were calculated using the lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) using Kenward-Roger’s approximation for the denominator degrees of freedom. Pairwise comparisons between the treatment groups were computed using the emmeans package (Lenth, 2025).

Important

Wollen wir Satterthwaite oder Kenward-Roger (konservativer in der Schätung) verwenden?

2 Results

2.1 Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics of students’ demographic characteristics and pre-test scores are presented in Table 1.

We found significant differences between the treatment groups at the pretest in terms of gender distribution, age, and graduate level (see Table 1). Therefore, we included these variables as covariates in the subsequent analyses.

The descriptive statistics of students’ change in the outcome measures over time per treatment group are listed in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

2.2 Linear Mixed-Effects Models

We will report the main effects of the treatment groups (i.e., control vs. STEM and language seminar, control vs. STEM seminar, control vs. language seminar, and STEM vs. language seminar).

The results of the linear mixed-effects models for each outcome measure are presented in Table 2 and Table 3.

2.2.1 AI Literacy

We did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in AI literacy, \(F(2, 72.89) = 1.31\), \(p = .277\). Neither did the control group’s change differ significantly from both intervention groups, \(b = 1.33\), \(SE = 0.97\), \(t(73.78) = 1.38\), \(p = = .173\), nor did the change differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.68\), \(SE = 0.98\), \(t(72.09) = -0.69\), \(p = = .492\).

2.2.2 Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics

For all subscales related to Intelligent TPACK and EI ethics, that is, Intelligent TK, Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TCK, Intelligent TPACK, and AI ethics, we found a significant main effect of treatment on student’ change on the respective subscales. We found significantly higher increases in students’ Intelligent TPACK subscales in both intervention groups compared to the control group, whereas the intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, see ?@tbl-lmer-summary for an overview.

2.2.2.1 Intelligent TK

We found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in intelligent TK, \(F(2, 72.76) = 16.50\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ intelligent TK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 1.16\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.57) = 5.74\), \(p = < .001\), while the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = 0.19\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(72.02) = 0.95\), \(p = = .346\).

2.2.3 Intelligent TPK

We found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in intelligent TCK, \(F(2, 73.23) = 20.08\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ intelligent TCK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 1.26\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(74.31) = 6.33\), \(p = < .001\), whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly in their change, \(b = 0.19\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(72.28) = 0.94\), \(p = = .349\).

2.2.4 Intelligent TCK

We found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in intelligent TPK, \(F(2, 73.35) = 11.81\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ intelligent TPK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 0.98\), \(SE = 0.21\), \(t(74.49) = 4.78\), \(p = < .001\), but the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.07\), \(SE = 0.21\), \(t(72.35) = -0.34\), \(p = = .736\).

2.2.5 Intelligent TPACK

For all subscales of the Intelligent TPACK, that is, students’ TPACK knowledge, their perceived competence in integrating AI tools teaching their subject, and their perceived competence of applying generative AI in teaching their subject, we found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change on the respective subscales, TPACK knowledge: \(F(2, 73.25) = 19.84\), \(p < .001\), TPACK competence: \(F(2, 73.15) = 24.25\), \(p < .001\), and TPACK related to generative AI: \(F(2, 73.58) = 13.65\), \(p < .001\).

For all subscales, we found the same pattern that students’ Intelligent TPACK subscales differed significantly between the control group and the two intervention groups, with students in the intervention groups having a significantly higher increase than the control group, whereas the intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other. That is, for TPACK knoweldge: \(b = 1.37\), \(SE = 0.22\), \(t(74.34) = 6.29\), \(p = < .001\) and \(b = 0.07\), \(SE = 0.22\), \(t(72.30) = 0.33\), \(p = = .743\); TPACK competence: \(b = 1.47\), \(SE = 0.21\), \(t(74.18) = 6.96\), \(p = < .001\) and \(b = 0.13\), \(SE = 0.21\), \(t(72.24) = 0.59\), \(p = = .557\); and TPACK related to generative AI, \(b = 1.36\), \(SE = 0.26\), \(t(74.86) = 5.21\), \(p = < .001\) and \(b = 0.03\), \(SE = 0.27\), \(t(72.49) = 0.13\), \(p = = .900\).

2.2.6 AI Ethics

For ethics related to the use of AI in education, we found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in XYZ, \(F(2, 73.82) = 16.80\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ XYZ in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 1.46\), \(SE = 0.25\), \(t(75.24) = 5.75\), \(p = < .001\), whereas the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = 0.34\), \(SE = 0.26\), \(t(72.63) = 1.32\), \(p = = .191\).

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

check_demo_vars <- function(
  data,
  demo_vars = c("age", "semester", "gender", "students"),
  id = "code",
  time_col = "time",
  pre_label = "pre",
  post_label = "post",
  show_only_diff = FALSE
) {
  out <- data %>%
    select(all_of(c(id, time_col, demo_vars))) %>%
    # ensure a common type across demo vars
    mutate(across(all_of(demo_vars), as.character)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = all_of(demo_vars),
      names_to = "variable",
      values_to = "value"
      # alternatively: values_transform = as.character
      # or: values_ptypes = list(value = character())
    ) %>%
    group_by(.data[[id]], variable, .data[[time_col]]) %>%
    summarise(
      value = paste(unique(na.omit(value)), collapse = ", "),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = all_of(time_col), values_from = value) %>%
    transmute(
      !!id := .data[[id]],
      variable,
      pre = .data[[pre_label]],
      post = .data[[post_label]],
      match = (pre == post) | (is.na(pre) & is.na(post))
    ) %>%
    arrange(.data[[id]], variable)

  if (show_only_diff) {
    out <- filter(out, is.na(match) | !match)
  }
  out
}
check_demo_vars(
  data,
  demo_vars = c("age", "semester", "gender", "students"),
  id = "code",
  show_only_diff = T
)
